title: Adenomyosis
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, causing a uniformly enlarged, tender uterus and heavy, painful periods. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion and imaging, especially ultrasound, with MRI as a confirmatory tool when available.

sections.p: Adenomyosis is a benign invasion of endometrial tissue into the uterine muscle, leading to a diffusely enlarged uterus. Diagnosis requires a combination of history, pelvic exam, and imaging.
b: Diffuse uterine enlargement >12 weeks size
Tender, boggy uterus on bimanual exam
Heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) and dysmenorrhoea

t.b: Is adenomyosis likely? – Shows heterogeneous myometrium, myometrial cysts, or a thickened junctional zone; supports diagnosis when MRI unavailable.
Does the uterus have characteristic features? – Improves resolution of junctional zone thickening (>12 mm) and myometrial cysts.
What is the definitive imaging? – Demonstrates junctional zone >12 mm, high‑signal foci on T2; used when ultrasound equivocal.

sections.p: No universally accepted staging; clinicians grade severity by symptom burden and uterine size.
b: Mild: <12 weeks uterine size, minimal impact on daily life
Moderate: 12‑16 weeks size, anemia or work‑loss
Severe: >16 weeks size, refractory bleeding, anemia, or infertility

sections.p: Exact cause is unknown; risk factors are hormonal and structural.
b: Multiparity and prior uterine surgery (C‑section, myomectomy)
Age 35‑50 years, especially in women with prolonged estrogen exposure
Co‑existing fibroids or endometriosis
In low‑resource settings, chronic use of herbal uterotonics may contribute

sections.p: Patients present with a triad of heavy menstrual bleeding, dysmenorrhoea, and a uniformly enlarged, tender uterus.
b: Painful periods that may start later in reproductive life
Dyspareunia or chronic pelvic pressure

sections.p: Imaging is central; labs assess anemia and rule out other causes.
b: CBC – detects iron‑deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss
Serum ferritin – confirms iron stores

t.b: Is the patient anemic? – Low hemoglobin/Hct indicates need for iron therapy before definitive treatment.
Are iron stores depleted? – Ferritin <30 µg/L confirms iron deficiency.
Is there co‑existent hyperplasia or cancer? – Excludes malignancy when bleeding is irregular or post‑menopausal.

sections.p: Complications arise from chronic blood loss and uterine distortion.
b: Severe anemia (Hb <8 g/dL) requiring transfusion
Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss
Rarely, uterine rupture in late pregnancy

sections.p: Treatment is symptom‑driven, balancing fertility desires and resource availability.
b: First‑line: NSAIDs for dysmenorrhoea; combined oral contraceptives (COC) to suppress ectopic endometrium
If COC unavailable: progestogen‑only pills or injectable depot medroxyprogesterone acetate
For refractory cases: uterine‑sparing surgery (adenomyomectomy) where expertise exists, otherwise hysterectomy

t.b: Will they relieve pain? – Reduce prostaglandin‑mediated cramps; avoid in active peptic ulcer disease.
Will it control bleeding? – Suppresses ovulation and endometrial proliferation; avoid in smokers >35 y or thrombo‑risk.
Can it reduce bleeding locally? – Provides high‑dose progestin to the endometrium; contraindicated in active infection.

sections.p: Regular review of symptom control, anemia status, and uterine size.
b: Re‑evaluate every 3‑6 months; repeat CBC
Counsel on limiting unnecessary uterine instrumentation
Encourage iron‑rich diet and supplementation

sections.p: Conditions sharing heavy bleeding and uterine enlargement.
b: Uterine fibroids (leiomyoma) – focal masses, irregular contour
Endometrial hyperplasia – thickened endometrium without myometrial invasion
Endometriosis – pain out of proportion to bleeding, no uterine enlargement

sections.p: Imaging and labs may be deceptive in low‑resource settings.
b: Ultrasound may miss subtle junctional zone thickening; MRI is more sensitive but often unavailable
Normal CBC can mask chronic low‑grade blood loss; always assess ferritin

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anemia (Hb <8 g/dL) with dizziness or tachycardia
Sudden worsening pelvic pain suggesting torsion or rupture

faq.q: Why does adenomyosis cause a uniformly enlarged uterus?
faq.a: Endometrial tissue within the myometrium expands the muscle diffusely, unlike fibroids which form discrete nodules.

faq.q: Can adenomyosis be cured without hysterectomy?
faq.a: Symptoms can be controlled medically; definitive cure usually requires hysterectomy, though adenomyomectomy is an option in selected cases.
Yes, distorted uterine architecture and abnormal contractility can impair implantation and increase miscarriage risk.

exam: What bedside findings would raise suspicion for adenomyosis versus fibroids? — Uniformly tender, boggy uterus without discrete nodules suggests adenomyosis; fibroids feel firm, irregular.
A 38‑year‑old with heavy bleeding has a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL. What is your immediate management? — Stabilize with iron and consider transfusion; start NSAIDs/COC while arranging imaging.
How does a thickened junctional zone on ultrasound help differentiate adenomyosis? — Junctional zone >12 mm is characteristic for adenomyosis; fibroids do not affect this layer.
Why might a combined oral contraceptive be contraindicated in this patient? — If she smokes >15 cigarettes/day or has a history of thromboembolism, COC increases clot risk.
In a setting without MRI, what ultrasound features are most reliable for adenomyosis? — Myometrial cysts, heterogeneous myometrium, and a globular uterus are key clues.
What are the key red‑flag complications that require urgent referral? — Severe anemia, uncontrolled hemorrhage, or sudden severe pelvic pain indicating possible uterine rupture.
Explain why a levonorgestrel IUS may be preferred over systemic progestins in some patients. — Provides high local progestin with minimal systemic side effects; avoids daily pill adherence.

How would you counsel a woman desiring future fertility about adenomyosis treatment options? — Discuss medical suppression first, then fertility‑preserving surgery if symptoms persist, highlighting risks of recurrence.
